claims.text: TruthfulQA is a benchmark consisting of 817 questions across 38 categories including health, law, finance, and politics.
claims.reason: The paper abstract and Section 1.1 explicitly state '817 questions that span 38 categories, including health, law, finance and politics'.

claims.text: GPT-judge is a fine-tuned GPT-3-6.7B model developed to classify generated answers as true or false.
claims.reason: Section 3.2 states 'GPT-judge is a GPT-3-6.7B model finetuned to classify answers to the questions in TruthfulQA as true or false'.

claims.text: GPT-judge was trained on approximately 22.4k examples consisting of 6.9k reference answers and 15.5k human-labeled model outputs.
claims.reason: Section 3.2 and Appendix B.1 confirm the training set contains '6.9k examples where the answer is a true/false reference answer' and 'around 15.5k examples where the answer is generated by one of the models', totaling ~22.4k.

claims.text: The benchmark is evaluated in a true zero-shot setting, meaning no gradient updates or TruthfulQA examples were used in the prompts.
claims.reason: Section 3.1 defines true zero-shot as '(i) no gradient updates are performed and (ii) no examples from TruthfulQA appear in prompts'.

claims.text: Human judges assigned one of 13 qualitative labels to answers, which were then mapped to scalar truth scores in [0, 1].
claims.reason: Appendix D and Table 8 confirm that evaluators assign one of 13 qualitative labels (e.g., 'True: fact', 'Mostly true', 'False') each mapped to a scalar score in [0, 1].

claims.text: GPT-judge predicts human labels with 90-96% accuracy.
claims.reason: Section 4.4 states 'The finetuned GPT-judge model is able to predict human evaluations of truthfulness with 90-96% validation accuracy', and Table 1 shows per-model accuracies ranging from 0.798 to 0.962.
Section 4.1 states 'The human participant produced 94% true answers', and the abstract also states 'human performance was 94%'.

claims.text: The best-performing model (GPT-3-175B with helpful prompt) was truthful on only 58% of questions.
claims.reason: Section 4.1 states 'the best model (GPT-3-175B with helpful prompt) produced 58% true answers', corroborated in the abstract.

claims.text: The best model gave false and informative answers 42% of the time, compared to 6% for the human baseline.
claims.reason: Section 4.1 explicitly states 'This model also generated answers that were both false and informative 42% of the time (compared to 6% for the human baseline)'.

claims.text: Larger models were generally less truthful—an inverse scaling trend that contrasts with most NLP tasks where performance improves with model size.
claims.reason: Section 4.2 and Figure 2 demonstrate that 'larger models generally do worse than smaller models in the same family (inverse scaling)', contrasting with standard NLP scaling behavior.

claims.text: The benchmark and associated code are publicly available on GitHub.
claims.reason: Section 1.1 states 'The benchmark and code is available at https://github.com/sylinrl/TruthfulQA'.

claims.text: Models tested include GPT-3, GPT-Neo/J, GPT-2, and a T5-based model (UnifiedQA).
claims.reason: Section 3.1 lists all four model families: GPT-3, GPT-Neo/J, GPT-2, and UnifiedQA (T5-based), evaluated across different sizes.

claims.text: The authors suggest that simply increasing model size is less effective than using techniques like prompt engineering, reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), or information retrieval to improve factual accuracy.
claims.reason: Section 4.3 explicitly states 'we believe that scaling up is most promising in conjunction with other techniques such as prompt engineering or finetuning... fine-tuned by reinforcement learning from human feedback... combined with information retrieval'.
